title: Visuospatial Neglect: A Theory-Informed Overview of Current and Emerging Strategies and a Systematic Review on the Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is a multifaceted neuropsychological disorder characterized by a failure to attend to, report, or respond to stimuli in the contralesional space, most commonly the left hemispace following right hemisphere damage. This syndrome is not merely a sensory or motor deficit but reflects a profound disruption in spatial attention networks, wherein the brain's ability to orient and maintain awareness across the environment is impaired. The condition often manifests in daily activities such as reading, dressing, or navigation, highlighting its functional impact beyond laboratory testing.

Emerging evidence positions neglect as a disconnection syndrome, wherein damage to white matter tracts disrupts communication between key cortical regions involved in attentional control, rather than being solely attributable to focal gray matter lesions. This perspective is supported by neuroimaging studies that reveal distributed network dysfunction, implicating frontoparietal and subcortical pathways in the pathophysiology of spatial awareness deficits. The integration of structural and functional connectivity data underscores that neglect arises from the breakdown of large-scale attentional networks, not isolated cortical damage.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is increasingly recognized as a disorder involving disrupted spatial representation and remapping mechanisms, rather than a simple attentional deficit. Impairments in spatial remapping—particularly the ability to update the location of stimuli relative to self or eye position—contribute significantly to the persistence of neglect symptoms, especially in dynamic environments. Patients with chronic neglect often fail to integrate allocentric and egocentric reference frames, leading to mislocalization of objects even when visual input is intact. This deficit is distinct from primary sensory loss and reflects higher-order spatial processing dysfunction.

Emerging evidence suggests that white matter integrity, particularly in dorsal and ventral attention networks, plays a critical role in the chronicity of neglect. A longitudinal study demonstrated that lesions in the superior longitudinal fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus are strong predictors of persistent visual neglect, underscoring the importance of structural connectivity in recovery trajectories. Furthermore, vestibular dysfunction has been proposed as a contributing factor, with some patients exhibiting neglect-like symptoms following unilateral vestibular lesions, suggesting a multisensory integration deficit that extends beyond visual attention systems.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is not solely a disorder of spatial attention but also involves disruptions in multisensory integration and arousal systems that modulate spatial awareness. The influence of alertness on attentional processes has been shown to differentially affect spatial and nonspatial components of visual processing, with reduced alertness exacerbating neglect symptoms even in the absence of primary spatial deficits. This highlights the role of tonic arousal networks—particularly those involving the right frontal and parietal regions—in sustaining spatial orienting, and suggests that neglect may arise from a failure to maintain adequate vigilance for contralateral space rather than a pure perceptual deficit.

Furthermore, structural disconnection of white matter tracts, particularly those linking parietal, frontal, and subcortical regions, has been implicated in the persistence of neglect. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) tractography studies reveal that damage to the superior longitudinal fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus correlates strongly with the severity and chronicity of neglect, providing a neuroanatomical substrate for the disconnection hypothesis beyond cortical lesions alone.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is frequently accompanied by extinction, a phenomenon in which a patient fails to report a contralesional stimulus when presented simultaneously with an ipsilesional one, despite detecting it in isolation. This dissociation highlights the dynamic, competitive nature of spatial attention and suggests that neglect is not merely a deficit in sensory processing but a disruption in attentional prioritization. Ref [3] demonstrates that acute visual neglect and extinction represent distinct functional states of the visuospatial attention system, with extinction reflecting transient competition dynamics rather than permanent sensory loss, thereby informing models of attentional bias in neglect.

Beyond cortical lesions, subcortical structures such as the basal ganglia play a critical role in the emergence of neglect, challenging the traditional focus on parietal cortex alone. Ref [4] employs normalized perfusion MRI to identify consistent patterns of hypoperfusion in the basal ganglia of patients with neglect, linking subcortical dysfunction to the behavioral syndrome and supporting a network-based model of spatial attention. These findings underscore that neglect arises from distributed network disruptions, not isolated cortical damage, and emphasize the need to consider subcortical contributions in both clinical assessment and therapeutic targeting.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Foundations and Clinical Characterization of Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is increasingly understood not merely as a deficit in spatial attention, but as a disruption in the brain's global orientation system, which integrates egocentric and allocentric reference frames to maintain a coherent representation of space. This integrative function is lateralized, with the right hemisphere playing a dominant role in sustaining spatial awareness across both hemispaces, as evidenced by the profound and persistent neglect symptoms following right-hemispheric lesions. The breakdown of this global spatial framework may underlie not only the failure to attend to contralesional space but also the misalignment of perceptual and motor coordinates essential for goal-directed behavior.

Emerging evidence suggests that oscillatory synchrony—particularly in the alpha and theta bands—serves as a dynamic mechanism for coordinating attentional networks across distributed cortical regions. Disruptions in these rhythmic patterns may contribute to the temporal instability of spatial representation observed in neglect patients, impairing the binding of sensory inputs into a unified spatial percept. Such neural synchrony deficits may explain why neglect symptoms fluctuate across tasks and contexts, reflecting a failure in the temporal coordination of attentional resources rather than a static lesion-induced deficit.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Spatial neglect is increasingly understood as a disorder of attentional networks rather than a simple sensory or motor deficit. The attention network model posits that spatial awareness relies on a distributed frontoparietal network, with the right hemisphere dominating attentional orienting toward contralateral space. Damage to this network—particularly in the right inferior parietal lobule or temporo-parietal junction—disrupts the balance between dorsal (goal-directed) and ventral (stimulus-driven) attention systems, leading to biased processing toward the ipsilesional side. This framework explains why neglect patients fail to orient to contralesional stimuli even in the absence of primary sensory loss.

Recent evidence from neuroimaging and lesion-symptom mapping further supports the role of structural disconnection in neglect, highlighting that white matter pathways linking parietal and frontal regions are critical for maintaining spatial attention. Disruption of these tracts, even in the absence of extensive cortical damage, can produce persistent neglect symptoms, underscoring the network-based nature of the disorder.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A growing body of evidence supports the view that spatial neglect may arise not only from cortical damage but also from disruptions in vestibular-visual integration, positioning it as a disorder of spatial orientation grounded in multisensory processing. The vestibular system, critical for encoding egocentric spatial coordinates, may contribute to neglect when its right-hemispheric projections are compromised, leading to a systematic bias in perceived midline and spatial attention. This framework suggests that neglect is not merely an attentional deficit but a disturbance in the brain’s representation of body-centered space, which can be exacerbated by lesions affecting vestibular cortical networks. Supporting this, ref [14] proposes that vestibular dysfunction underlies persistent neglect symptoms, particularly in cases where traditional attentional models fail to explain the full clinical profile.

Furthermore, the persistence of neglect in chronic stages may be linked to structural disconnections in white matter tracts that integrate vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive inputs, as highlighted by longitudinal findings in ref [11]. These data underscore the need for rehabilitation strategies that target multisensory recalibration, such as vestibular stimulation or prism adaptation, which may restore allocentric and egocentric spatial mappings by engaging residual network integrity.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
The interhemispheric rivalry model posits that spatial neglect arises from an imbalance in attentional control between the two hemispheres, with the intact hemisphere exerting excessive inhibition over the damaged one. This framework has motivated interventions aimed at restoring interhemispheric equilibrium, such as non-invasive brain stimulation targeting the contralesional parietal cortex. However, the neural substrates underlying this imbalance extend beyond cortical regions to include white matter pathways critical for interhemispheric communication. DTI-MR tractography studies have demonstrated that disruptions in the corpus callosum and superior longitudinal fasciculus correlate strongly with the severity and persistence of neglect symptoms, suggesting that structural disconnection contributes significantly to the functional asymmetry observed in neglect patients ref [4].

Furthermore, the role of subcortical and multisensory integration systems in modulating attentional bias has gained traction, particularly through the lens of vestibular contributions to spatial orientation. The vestibular system, traditionally associated with postural control, also plays a pivotal role in anchoring spatial representations and modulating attentional weighting across hemispace. Evidence suggests that vestibular stimulation can transiently ameliorate neglect by recalibrating internal spatial maps, implicating this system as a key node in the network underlying spatial awareness ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Multisensory integration deficits represent a critical dimension in the theoretical framing of spatial neglect, particularly in how cross-modal interactions modulate attentional biases. Emerging evidence suggests that prior multisensory experiences can recalibrate unisensory processing streams, potentially offering a mechanistic basis for rehabilitation strategies that leverage congruent auditory or tactile cues to reorient attention toward neglected space. This principle is supported by findings that non-spatial sensory inputs can dynamically influence the weighting of spatial representations, thereby mitigating asymmetries in attentional allocation. The interplay between sensory history and spatial awareness underscores the potential of multisensory training protocols to induce neuroplastic changes beyond traditional visual-only approaches.

Furthermore, the clinical heterogeneity of neglect is closely tied to lesion topography and its impact on distributed networks governing multisensory integration. Mapping studies have highlighted the parietal lobe’s central role in integrating spatial information across modalities, with disruptions in this region correlating with persistent neglect symptoms that resist unimodal interventions. The predictive value of lesion location, combined with multisensory processing deficits, reinforces the need for theory-driven, multimodal rehabilitation paradigms that target the underlying network dysfunction rather than isolated behavioral symptoms.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.subsection_title: Theoretical Models Informing Neglect Rehabilitation - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Subtopic 5 examines the role of crossmodal predictive processing and multisensory integration in neglect, emphasizing how disrupted temporal and spatial alignment of sensory inputs contributes to attentional biases. Emerging evidence suggests that neglect patients exhibit impaired integration of audiovisual signals, particularly when stimuli are asynchronous or spatially incongruent, leading to a failure in updating internal spatial representations. This deficit is not merely perceptual but reflects a breakdown in predictive coding mechanisms that normally bind multisensory events into coherent perceptual objects. The role of crossmodal prediction in emotional and spatial perception further underscores its relevance, as neglect may involve a failure to anticipate and integrate salient crossmodal cues that guide orienting behavior.

Ref [27] demonstrates that crossmodal prediction is critical for audiovisual emotion perception, a process that may be compromised in neglect due to right-hemisphere dominance in integrating affective and spatial signals. Similarly, ref [21] reveals that cortical mechanisms underlying mental imagery and embodied simulation—key components of spatial representation—are modulated by multisensory inputs, suggesting that neglect rehabilitation should target the re-establishment of predictive, grounded representations of space. Together, these findings support interventions that train predictive multisensory integration to recalibrate spatial attention.

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Current non-stimulation interventions for visuospatial neglect increasingly target the underlying network dysfunctions rather than isolated behavioral symptoms. A growing body of evidence supports the view that neglect arises not merely from focal cortical damage but from disrupted connectivity within distributed attention networks, particularly those involving the right parietal, frontal, and subcortical regions. This network-based perspective has informed rehabilitation strategies that aim to re-engage or recalibrate these distributed systems through environmental and cognitive restructuring. For instance, interventions leveraging prism adaptation or visual scanning training implicitly rely on the brain’s capacity for adaptive reorganization within these compromised networks, as highlighted by models of neglect as a disconnection syndrome.

The role of white matter disconnections in sustaining neglect has been further elucidated by multimodal neuroimaging studies, which demonstrate that structural integrity of fronto-parietal and interhemispheric tracts critically determines both the severity and persistence of neglect symptoms. These findings underscore the rationale for interventions that promote compensatory network dynamics, such as cueing paradigms and virtual reality-based exploration, which may facilitate functional reintegration of segregated nodes. The convergence of clinical observation and network neuroscience thus provides a robust theoretical foundation for non-stimulation approaches that prioritize system-level recovery over localized symptom suppression.

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Emerging theoretical frameworks increasingly position visuospatial neglect not merely as a perceptual deficit but as a disorder of spatial representation and remapping. Impairments in the ability to update or maintain spatial coordinates relative to self or environment—termed spatial remapping deficits—may underlie persistent neglect symptoms even when primary sensory or attentional systems are partially intact. This perspective is supported by evidence that patients with neglect exhibit disrupted internal representations of space, independent of oculomotor or sensory input, suggesting a higher-order cognitive component to the disorder. Such remapping failures may explain why some patients fail to attend to contralesional space even after visual scanning training, as the internal spatial map remains distorted.

Notably, the contribution of spatial remapping impairments to unilateral visual neglect has been empirically demonstrated in studies linking neglect severity to dysfunction in parietal and frontal networks responsible for coordinate transformation, rather than solely to sensory extinction or attentional bias ref [24]. Furthermore, recent longitudinal data suggest that vestibular system dysfunction may interact with these remapping deficits, potentially destabilizing egocentric reference frames and exacerbating spatial disorientation ref [14]. These insights are guiding novel rehabilitation strategies that target internal spatial representation through mental imagery, virtual reality-based spatial retraining, and multisensory integration protocols.

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Non-stimulation interventions targeting visuospatial neglect increasingly recognize the role of multisensory and vestibular integration in spatial orientation. The vestibular system, traditionally associated with postural control, contributes significantly to the allocation of spatial attention and the internal representation of egocentric space. Emerging evidence suggests that vestibular stimulation—via caloric irrigation or galvanic stimulation—can transiently ameliorate neglect symptoms by modulating cortical networks involved in spatial awareness, potentially through interactions with the temporo-parietal junction and insular cortex. This mechanism underscores the vestibular system’s broader role beyond balance, influencing attentional biases in both healthy individuals and stroke patients with neglect ref [26].

Furthermore, the interplay between alertness and spatial attention is critical in shaping neglect phenomenology. Deficits in tonic alertness can exacerbate spatial inattention, particularly in the contralesional field, independent of primary perceptual impairments. Interventions that enhance alertness through auditory or visual cues have demonstrated efficacy in improving detection of contralesional stimuli, highlighting the need to disentangle spatial from nonspatial attentional components in rehabilitation design ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Non-stimulation interventions for visuospatial neglect increasingly recognize the interplay between neglect, extinction, and anosognosia as critical determinants of functional outcome. These clinical phenomena are not merely behavioral symptoms but reflect distinct functional states within the visuospatial attention network, each with unique neural correlates and rehabilitation implications. For instance, acute visual neglect and extinction have been shown to represent separable disruptions in attentional selection and awareness, suggesting that therapeutic strategies must be tailored to the specific attentional deficit profile rather than applied uniformly. Furthermore, the presence of anosognosia—lack of awareness of deficits—significantly moderates response to rehabilitation, as patients with impaired self-monitoring are less likely to engage with or benefit from conventional compensatory training.

Recent evidence underscores that lesion location, combined with the presence of extinction and anosognosia, robustly predicts impairment in activities of daily living after right-hemispheric stroke, highlighting the need for multimodal assessment prior to intervention selection. Mapping the functional neuroanatomy of neglect further reveals that distributed parietal and fronto-subcortical networks underlie these clinical profiles, implying that effective non-stimulation therapies must target network-level dysfunction rather than isolated perceptual deficits.

subsections.section_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Current and Emerging Non-Stimulation Interventions for Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Emerging theoretical frameworks increasingly emphasize the role of large-scale neural dynamics in visuospatial neglect, particularly the disruption of oscillatory synchrony across attentional networks. Ref [30] proposes that impaired phase-locking between frontal and parietal regions underlies the failure to allocate attention to contralesional space, suggesting that rehabilitation strategies targeting temporal coordination—such as rhythmic sensory entrainment or biofeedback—may restore functional connectivity without direct neuromodulation. This perspective shifts focus from structural lesions to dynamic network dysfunction, offering novel avenues for non-invasive, behaviorally grounded interventions.

Furthermore, the concept of global spatial orientation, as articulated in ref [25], highlights the lateralized organization of spatial representation systems, where right-hemisphere dominance governs allocentric and egocentric reference frame integration. Interventions that recalibrate these reference frames through multisensory integration tasks or virtual reality-based spatial reorientation may therefore address core deficits in spatial awareness beyond mere visual scanning. Together, these theoretical advances support a paradigm shift toward dynamic, network-based rehabilitation strategies that complement traditional compensatory approaches.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
The neurobiological basis of visuospatial neglect is rooted in distributed attention networks, particularly those involving the right parietal and frontal cortices, which mediate spatial orienting and attentional control. Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) strategies aim to rebalance interhemispheric competition by modulating activity in these networks, often targeting the contralesional parietal cortex to reduce pathological inhibition of the lesioned hemisphere. The functional relevance of the right parietal lobe in spatial attention is underscored by studies demonstrating that transient disruption via rTMS induces ipsilateral enhancements in visual spatial attention, mimicking aspects of neglect recovery through compensatory mechanisms.

Furthermore, the conceptualization of neglect as a disconnection syndrome highlights the importance of white matter integrity in sustaining attentional networks, suggesting that NIBS efficacy may depend not only on gray matter stimulation but also on the functional connectivity of underlying tracts. These insights inform protocol design by emphasizing the need to align stimulation targets with network-level dysfunction rather than focal lesions alone.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
The neuroanatomical substrates of visuospatial neglect significantly influence the target selection and efficacy of non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) protocols. Lesion mapping studies have demonstrated that chronic neglect is strongly associated with white matter disruptions in dorsal attention networks, particularly involving the superior longitudinal fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, which compromise interregional communication critical for spatial awareness. These structural deficits underscore the need for NIBS protocols to account for individual variability in white matter integrity, as lesions in these tracts predict persistent neglect despite cortical stimulation. Furthermore, emerging evidence suggests that neglect may arise not solely from cortical dysfunction but from disrupted spatial remapping mechanisms, implicating parietal and frontal regions in the dynamic updating of spatial representations during eye movements and attentional shifts.

Targeting these remapping deficits requires stimulation protocols that modulate the balance between hemispheric dominance in spatial processing, particularly by enhancing right parietal activity or suppressing maladaptive left hemisphere overactivity. The heterogeneity in lesion profiles, as characterized in acute left hemisphere stroke populations, further necessitates personalized stimulation approaches that integrate structural imaging to identify viable cortical targets and avoid stimulating regions with extensive underlying white matter damage.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
The neurophysiological effects of non-invasive brain stimulation in visuospatial neglect are closely tied to the modulation of cortical excitability and oscillatory dynamics within attentional networks. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), for instance, can induce transient 'virtual lesions' or enhance neural activity in targeted regions, thereby revealing causal roles of parietal and frontal nodes in spatial attention. Research has demonstrated that TMS-induced changes in perception are mediated by alterations in interhemispheric balance and local gamma-band synchronization, directly influencing the salience mapping of contralesional space ref [27].

In contrast, transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) has been explored for its ability to entrain endogenous oscillations, yet its efficacy in modulating spatial attention remains limited. A recent study applying high-gamma tACS over primary visual cortex (V1) improved contrast sensitivity but failed to alter spatial attentional biases, suggesting that low-level perceptual enhancements do not necessarily translate to higher-order spatial neglect remediation ref [31]. This dissociation underscores the need for protocol designs that target network-level dynamics rather than isolated sensory processing areas.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
The efficacy of non-invasive brain stimulation in modulating visuospatial neglect is critically dependent on targeting the underlying neuroanatomical and functional disruptions that define the disorder. Lesion mapping studies have demonstrated that basal ganglia dysfunction, often overlooked in favor of parietal focus, contributes significantly to neglect phenotypes, as revealed by normalized perfusion MRI identifying consistent hypoperfusion patterns in subcortical regions among neglect patients ref [4]. Furthermore, the heterogeneity of neglect presentation—ranging from perceptual extinction to anosognosia—underscores the need for protocol personalization, as lesion location and comorbid symptoms collectively predict functional impairment and response potential ref [15]. These findings argue against one-size-fits-all stimulation protocols and advocate for neuroimaging-guided targeting that accounts for both cortical and subcortical network contributions to spatial attention failure.

Emerging protocol designs must therefore integrate multimodal neuroimaging to delineate individualized network dysfunction, moving beyond conventional parietal stimulation targets. The convergence of perfusion abnormalities in basal ganglia and lesion-site-dependent symptom profiles suggests that stimulation efficacy may be enhanced by tailoring intensity, frequency, and coil placement to the patient’s specific neurovascular and structural signature, thereby aligning neuromodulation with the pathophysiological substrate of each case.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: Modalities, Mechanisms, and Protocol Design - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
The efficacy of non-invasive brain stimulation in modulating visuospatial neglect may be fundamentally linked to the restoration of oscillatory dynamics underlying attentional allocation. Emerging evidence suggests that abnormal synchrony in theta and gamma frequency bands disrupts the integration of spatial information across hemispheres, contributing to attentional asymmetry. Targeted transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) aimed at rebalancing interhemispheric oscillatory coherence offers a mechanistically grounded approach to rehabilitation, potentially reinstating the temporal precision required for spatial awareness.

Furthermore, the lateralized organization of spatial processing, as described in the framework of global orientation in space, implies that stimulation protocols must account for hemispheric asymmetries in functional dominance. Interventions that selectively enhance right parietal excitability or suppress maladaptive left-hemisphere overactivity must be calibrated not only to anatomical targets but also to the dynamic, frequency-specific signatures of attentional networks.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) interventions in visuospatial neglect are grounded in the understanding that spatial attention is mediated by distributed cortical networks, particularly involving the right parietal and frontal lobes. Studies using repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) to induce transient 'virtual lesions' in the parietal cortex have demonstrated that suppression of contralateral attentional processing can replicate neglect-like behaviors, thereby validating the causal role of these regions in spatial awareness. Importantly, such experiments reveal that rTMS-induced disruption leads to enhanced attention ipsilaterally, suggesting a competitive interhemispheric balance model that underpins neglect pathology.

This interhemispheric rivalry framework is further supported by evidence linking structural disconnections in white matter tracts to functional impairments in spatial attention, highlighting that neglect arises not merely from focal gray matter lesions but from disrupted network integrity. The convergence of functional and structural data underscores the necessity of targeting network dynamics rather than isolated brain regions in NIBS protocols.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
The heterogeneity in lesion topography underlying visuospatial neglect significantly influences response to non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS), necessitating lesion-based stratification in clinical trials. Recent evidence highlights that acute left hemisphere strokes frequently give rise to right hemispatial neglect, with distinct clinical profiles tied to the extent and location of cortical and subcortical damage ref [34]. This underscores the importance of accounting for lesion characteristics—such as involvement of the inferior parietal lobule or temporo-parietal junction—when interpreting NIBS outcomes, as these regions are critical nodes in the dorsal and ventral attention networks targeted by stimulation protocols.

Furthermore, the persistence of neglect into the chronic phase is strongly predicted by white matter disruptions, particularly in the superior longitudinal fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, which impair inter-regional communication necessary for spatial awareness ref [8]. These structural deficits may limit the efficacy of NIBS that relies on intact network connectivity to modulate neural activity, suggesting that patients with extensive white matter damage may require alternative or adjunctive stimulation paradigms.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
The efficacy of non-invasive brain stimulation in modulating visuospatial neglect is partially contingent on the integrity of underlying neural circuits, particularly those involving visual and attentional processing networks. While rTMS and tDCS have demonstrated potential to rebalance interhemispheric inhibition, their effects may be constrained by the extent of white matter disconnection and cortical dysfunction. For instance, transcranial magnetic stimulation has been shown to directly influence perceptual thresholds and cortical excitability in visual areas, suggesting that its therapeutic impact may rely on restoring normal sensory processing rather than purely attentional reorienting ref [27]. Furthermore, studies using high-gamma transcranial alternating current stimulation over V1 have revealed a dissociation between contrast sensitivity enhancement and spatial attention modulation, indicating that stimulation targeting early visual cortex may improve perceptual input without rectifying the core attentional bias characteristic of neglect ref [31].

This distinction underscores the need for mechanistically informed stimulation protocols that account for both perceptual and attentional deficits. The co-occurrence of neglect with other spatial disorders, such as Balint’s syndrome and Gerstmann’s syndrome, further complicates the interpretation of stimulation outcomes, as overlapping neural substrates may contribute to heterogeneous clinical presentations ref [33]. Consequently, patient stratification based on lesion profiles and functional deficits—rather than diagnostic labels alone—may be essential to optimize therapeutic precision.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
The heterogeneity in lesion topography underlying visuospatial neglect complicates the interpretation of non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) outcomes, as distinct neural substrates may differentially respond to neuromodulation. Recent evidence suggests that basal ganglia involvement, often overlooked in traditional cortical-centric models, contributes significantly to neglect severity and may alter the efficacy of NIBS protocols targeting parietal or frontal regions. Normalized perfusion MRI has identified consistent hypoperfusion patterns in basal ganglia structures among neglect patients, implicating subcortical-thalamocortical circuits in the persistence of attentional deficits ref [4]. Furthermore, the functional interplay between neglect, extinction, and anosognosia underscores the need for patient stratification based on multimodal clinical profiles, as these comorbidities independently predict functional impairment and may modulate treatment response ref [15].

Mapping the functional neuroanatomy of spatial neglect reveals that parietal lobe dysfunction is not monolithic; rather, it encompasses dissociable subnetworks governing egocentric versus allocentric spatial coding, which may differentially engage with NIBS targets. This neuroanatomical complexity helps explain inconsistent therapeutic outcomes across studies that do not account for lesion location or network-level disruption ref [19]. Consequently, future NIBS trials must integrate high-resolution neuroimaging to match stimulation parameters with individualized network profiles, moving beyond population-level averages toward precision neuromodulation.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Review of Clinical Evidence for Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Visuospatial Neglect - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
The heterogeneity in clinical responses to non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) in visuospatial neglect may be partially explained by individual differences in the functional lateralization of spatial attention networks. The concept of global orientation in space, as proposed in ref [25], suggests that hemispheric asymmetries in spatial representation are not merely structural but reflect dynamic, distributed computations that vary across patients. This theoretical framework helps account for why some individuals exhibit robust improvement following right parietal inhibition, while others show minimal or paradoxical responses—potentially due to pre-existing compensatory reorganization or atypical lateralization. Such variability underscores the need for patient stratification based on neurofunctional profiles rather than lesion location alone.

Current NIBS protocols often assume a uniform pathophysiology of neglect, yet ref [25] implies that the efficacy of stimulation may depend on the integrity and dominance of spatial orienting systems that differ across individuals. Future trials should integrate neurocognitive phenotyping with NIBS to align stimulation targets with individualized spatial representation architectures, thereby enhancing therapeutic precision and reproducibility.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Advancing precision neurorehabilitation for visuospatial neglect requires a mechanistic understanding of attentional dysfunctions at the network level. Emerging evidence underscores the role of oscillatory dynamics in modulating attentional selection, particularly the suppression of unattended stimuli, which is impaired in neglect. Alpha oscillations, for instance, have been shown to correlate with the successful inhibition of distractors, suggesting their potential as a biomarker for attentional control deficits in neglect patients ref [10]. This insight opens avenues for neuromodulatory interventions that target specific frequency bands to restore inhibitory control.

Furthermore, the theoretical framework of attention as a distributed network, rather than a localized function, supports the need for personalized stimulation protocols that account for individual variations in network topology. The foundational work on brain mechanisms of attention provides a critical scaffold for identifying which nodes and connections are most predictive of treatment response, enabling stratification of patients based on neurophysiological profiles ref [23]. Integrating such biomarkers into adaptive trial designs will be essential for moving beyond one-size-fits-all approaches toward mechanism-informed, precision neurorehabilitation.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Precision neurorehabilitation for visuospatial neglect must account for the dynamic interplay between top-down attentional control and bottom-up sensory processing, which are differentially disrupted in neglect patients. Emerging evidence suggests that impaired top-down modulation of visual perception, rather than primary sensory deficits, underlies persistent spatial inattention, particularly in chronic cases. Functional connectivity analyses reveal that disrupted communication between frontoparietal networks and visual cortices correlates with failure to orient toward contralesional space, even when perceptual acuity is preserved. This highlights the need for interventions that selectively target these network-level dysfunctions, such as neurostimulation protocols calibrated to restore top-down biasing of visual processing.

Furthermore, the role of pre-saccadic attentional shifts—critical for spatial updating and target selection—appears compromised in neglect, contributing to oculomotor neglect and failure to integrate visual information across saccades. Restoring the temporal coordination of attentional preparation and eye movement execution may therefore represent a novel therapeutic target. Integrating eye-tracking biomarkers with adaptive stimulation protocols could enable real-time, individualized neuromodulation that reinforces intact attentional mechanisms during naturalistic visual exploration.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Precision neurorehabilitation for visuospatial neglect must account for the heterogeneity of underlying neural disruptions, particularly those involving multisensory integration and spatial representation beyond the visual modality. Emerging evidence suggests that vestibular dysfunction contributes significantly to the spatial bias in neglect, implicating the temporo-parietal junction and insular networks in integrating bodily and environmental reference frames. The vestibular system, traditionally viewed as a balance regulator, plays a critical role in anchoring spatial attention and body-centered coordinate systems, offering a novel target for neuromodulatory interventions. Furthermore, the dissociation between low-level perceptual deficits and higher-order attentional failures underscores the need for mechanistically stratified approaches, where interventions are matched to specific neurocognitive profiles rather than clinical syndromes alone.

Recent work distinguishing spatial neglect from related syndromes such as Balint’s and Gerstmann’s highlights the importance of differential diagnosis in tailoring rehabilitation strategies, as overlapping behavioral symptoms may arise from distinct network disruptions. A precision approach must therefore integrate neuroanatomical, functional, and behavioral biomarkers to identify subtypes amenable to vestibular stimulation, sensory reweighting, or crossmodal training.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Advancing precision neurorehabilitation for visuospatial neglect requires a deeper integration of functional neuroanatomical mapping to guide individualized intervention targets. Recent work has demonstrated that spatial neglect is not a unitary syndrome but arises from heterogeneous disruptions across distributed attention networks, with distinct contributions from parietal, frontal, and subcortical regions. Mapping the functional neuroanatomy of neglect reveals that lesion location alone is insufficient to predict behavioral profiles; instead, network-level dysfunction—particularly in the right intraparietal sulcus and temporoparietal junction—must be characterized to tailor neuromodulatory protocols effectively. Moreover, the interplay between neglect, extinction, and anosognosia underscores the need for multimodal biomarkers that capture both structural and functional states of the attention system.

Emerging evidence suggests that acute visual neglect and extinction reflect distinct functional states of the visuospatial attention system, implying that rehabilitation strategies must be stratified by underlying neural dynamics rather than clinical presentation alone. This calls for adaptive trial designs that incorporate real-time neuroimaging to monitor network reorganization and adjust stimulation parameters accordingly, moving beyond one-size-fits-all approaches toward mechanism-informed, patient-specific neurorehabilitation.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities
subsections.subsection_title: Future Directions: Precision Neurorehabilitation and Translational Priorities - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Future advances in precision neurorehabilitation for visuospatial neglect must account for the dynamic interplay between top-down expectations and sensory processing. Emerging evidence suggests that perceptual biases in neglect are not merely deficits in spatial attention but reflect disrupted internal models that predict sensory input based on prior context and meaning. Refining these models through theory-driven interventions could enable personalized stimulation protocols that recalibrate predictive coding in damaged networks. For instance, the modulation of alpha-band oscillations by meaningful stimuli—where perceptual expectations shape early visual responses—offers a mechanistic target for neuromodulation that goes beyond spatial cueing ref [10]. Similarly, fluctuations in instantaneous frequency as predictors of alpha amplitude reveal how temporal dynamics of neural oscillations gate perceptual awareness, suggesting that timing-sensitive stimulation protocols may restore rhythmic coordination in neglected space ref [11].

Integrating these neurophysiological signatures into adaptive trial designs could allow real-time adjustment of stimulation parameters based on individual oscillatory profiles, moving toward closed-loop neurorehabilitation. Such approaches would align with the growing consensus that neglect is not a static lesion effect but a dynamic state governed by predictive brain mechanisms ref [23].
